pages.text:
Code Comprehensor: Hierarchical Documentation
and Cross-Modal Retrieval for Large Repositories
Sujoy Roychowdhury∗, Joseph H. R. Isaac†, Jiangning Gao‡, Martin Klitte§ and Diarmuid Corcoran¶
Ericsson R&D
Email: {∗sujoy.roychowdhury, †joseph.isaac, ‡jiangning.gao, §martin.klitte, ¶diarmuid.corcoran}@ericsson.com
Abstract—Understanding large, complex, and rapidly evolving
code bases remains a core challenge for software engineering
at scale, hindering onboarding, maintenance, refactoring, and
impact analysis. Providing this information to a Large-Language
Model (LLM) is another hurdle, as the LLM must understand
not only the required code method but also its associated
methods in the grand scheme of the repository. We propose
Code Comprehensor, a hybrid retrieval–reasoning framework
combining (i) CodeGraph, a code dependency callgraph, (ii)
CodeScribe, which uses code-aware LLMs to generate hierar-
chical documentation across repository call graphs, and (iii)
CodeContrast, a CLIP-style dual-encoder model trained on
CodeScribe output to learn aligned text-code embeddings. Code-
Contrast enables fast, semantically precise retrieval of relevant
code-context neighborhoods, which serve as grounded evidence
for an MCP-based LLM orchestrator answering domain-specific
queries. Evaluation on OpenCV and a proprietary 5M-LOC
repository shows that CodeScribe-derived supervision signifi-
cantly improves cross-modal retrieval in text-to-code accuracy
over baseline approaches. Richer textual supervision (hierarchi-
cal documentation, parent/sibling context, and LLM-generated
synthetic questions) consistently enhances performance across
both repositories. LLM-as-a-judge evaluation using the popular
RAGAS of the Code Comprehensor output yields above 90%
faithfulness scores.
Index Terms—Large Language Models (LLMs), Code com-
prehension, Semantic code retrieval, Contrastive learning, CLIP-
style encoders, Software repository analysis, Program analysis,
Hybrid retrieval-reasoning frameworks
I. INTRODUCTION
Enterprises typically have large code repositories that have
been developed and maintained over the years. The ability to
document and understand such complex repositories has been
a challenge [1], [2]. Code complexity creates dependencies
on senior engineers’ expertise to understand and navigate
such repositories, and introduces inefficiencies in the Software
Development Life Cycle (SDLC) [3]. The growth of Large
Language Models (LLM) in recent years and their ability
to understand and explain code introduce the possibility of
making this process more efficient [4]. This growth will
lead to greater productivity in developing new features and
maintaining and debugging existing ones.
However, the ability to use LLMs to document and un-
derstand large repositories in a reliable, replicable fashion
requires careful design and consideration. Despite the large
context window of many modern LLMs [5], code repositories
often will consume a much larger number of tokens. For
example, [6] gives Lines of Code (LOC) for some public
repositories, and token sizes will be much larger. Proprietary
code repositories are often large in terms of LOC. For example,
one of the repositories mentioned in this paper is larger than
most listed in [6]. More importantly, just because an LLM
can process a large number of tokens does not mean an
LLM should access the entire repository for every question.
In addition to cost implications, large context sizes are known
to give poorer results [7], [8].
Additionally, code repositories often contain identical or
very similar files, methods, and variables across different
parts of the code base, and using probabilistic machinery
like an LLM is unlikely to be reliable or replicable. In
view of this, it is important to design systems that enable
LLMs to navigate code repositories more consistently and
deterministically. Regarding this issue, some studies discuss
using the inherent structure of code, as captured in the call
graph, to drive documentation. Work by [9] discusses using
a static-analysis-based call tree to generate documentation
for large-scale repositories recursively. A similar approach
to generate initial and incremental documentation has been
followed by other works [10]. A hierarchical engine for
document generation and querying has also been studied [11].
Recently, Google released a repository to document code [12];
however, to the best of our knowledge, the system’s design has
not been disclosed. The common aspect of these repositories
is the use of either the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) [13] or the
call-graph. However, if one wants to build more than just static
documentation, a broader and more comprehensive approach
is needed. Previous work [14], [15] has looked at cross-modal
contrastive learning for code search; however, without deep
domain-level documentation mapping methods to domain and
code structure, the effectiveness of such cross-modal retrieval
on large, complex repositories is limited.
A. Proposed Solution
We present Code Comprehensor, an end-to-end system
that combines four main components: (i) CodeGraph, a
call graph generated via static analysis and exposed through
API endpoints for traversal and chunking; (ii) CodeScribe, a
hierarchical documentation engine that recursively processes
directory-structured code, supports multiple documentation
chapters and custom prompts per directory, and outputs Plan-
tUML diagrams; (iii) a custom data processing module that
parses CodeScribe output into relational records linking meth-
ods to parent/sibling context; and (iv) CodeContrast, a CLIP-

CodeScribe operates on a repository directory structure with
configurable chapter-based perspectives (e.g., code description,
algorithms, data flow). For each start method (in-degree zero
in the method subgraph), CodeScribe retrieves the Depth-
First-Search (DFS) traversal tree via CodeGraph, chunks it
if necessary using post-order traversal to preserve hierarchy,
and generates documentation. CodeScribe supports both full
and incremental (git-commit-driven) documentation runs.
CodeContrast leverages the structured training data from
CodeScribe parsing to train a retrieval model. We adopt CLIP’s
dual-encoder architecture for efficient pre-computed embed-
dings and asymmetric modalities. The InfoNCE objective
learns well-separated embedding spaces and extends naturally
to multi-positive scenarios.
Finally, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) based orches-
tration layer integrates CodeGraph, CodeScribe, and Code-
Contrast into an agentic system accessible via an Integrated
Development Environment (IDE). This Master Agent invokes
specialized agents (RAG over CodeScribe output, CodeGraph
traversal, CodeContrast retrieval) to answer domain-specific
queries on code repositories.
The core contributions of this paper are as follows:
• A post-order chunking algorithm that enables LLM doc-
umentation of arbitrarily large call trees while preserving
structural hierarchy.
• A multi-granularity training data construction pipeline
that leverages parent-sibling relationships from documen-
tation structure and LLM-generated synthetic questions
for enhanced retrieval performance.
• Code Comprehensor: an integrated end-to-end system
combining CodeGraph, CodeScribe, and CodeContrast
components for large-scale repository understanding and
retrieval.
• Empirical
evidence
that
hierarchical
documentation-
derived supervision improves cross-modal code retrieval
by at least 9% Top-1 accuracy over baseline approaches.
The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. We
briefly summarize previous work in Section II. We discuss the
System Architecture in Section III, the detailed methodology
in Section IV, and present results in Section V. We conclude
with a discussion, threats to validity, and future works in
Sections VI, VII, and VIII, respectively.
II. RELATED WORK
A. Code Search and Retrieval
Code search and retrieval has been an active area of research
for understanding large repositories. Recent work has focused
on neural approaches combining text and code embeddings.
Sun et al. [16] presented context-aware code translation for
code search, while Chai et al. [17] explored cross-domain
deep code search using meta-learning techniques. Mathew and
Stolee [18] investigated cross-language code search, and Mao
et al. [19] proposed self-supervised query reformulation for
improved retrieval. More recently, Wang et al. [20] exam-
ined fusion of multiple code searchers, and Shi et al. [21]
introduced CoCoSoDa for effective contrastive learning on
code search tasks. Large-scale contrastive pre-training for code
retrieval has been explored by Li et al. [22], who developed
CodeRetriever. Comprehensive surveys on code search have
been provided by Di Grazia and Pradel [23] and Sun et al. [24].
B. Repository-Level Documentation Generation
Documentation generation at repository scale has emerged
as a critical need for understanding complex systems. Luo
et al. [25] introduced RepoAgent, which combines static

analysis with LLM-driven documentation. Hoang et al. [26]
developed CodeWiki, a framework for generating hierarchical
documentation. Sounthiraraj et al. [27] proposed a hierarchical
engine for structured document generation and querying.
C. Contrastive Learning for Code
Contrastive learning has proven effective for learning
aligned embeddings of code and text. Neelakantan et al. [28]
introduced text and code embeddings using contrastive meth-
ods. Li et al. [22] leveraged contrastive learning in CodeRe-
triever for large-scale pre-training. Shi et al. [21] proposed
CoCoSoDa with a momentum encoder design.
D. Differentiation from Prior Work
Code Comprehensor extends prior work in three key ways.
First, unlike code search methods that operate on isolated
code snippets (e.g., CodeRetriever, CoCoSoDa), our system
first generates hierarchical documentation that captures inter-
method relationships through call graph analysis and multi-
perspective documentation generation, then trains a contrastive
model on this enriched representation. Prior work on code
retrieval has focused primarily on Python and Java; CodeRe-
triever and CoCoSoDa lack publicly available implementations
for C/C++ repositories, limiting direct empirical comparison
on the systems programming domain where our work is
evaluated. Second, unlike RepoAgent, which focuses solely
on documentation generation, our system uses the generated
documentation as a structured training signal for a retrieval
model, enabling efficient inference-time retrieval without re-
quiring LLM calls per query. Third, we employ a post-order
chunking algorithm to handle arbitrarily large call trees while
preserving structural hierarchy, enabling scalable documenta-
tion and retrieval on repositories exceeding 5M lines of code.
III. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE
Figure 1 shows the overall system architecture for Code
Comprehensor. Git repositories are first cloned into our sys-
tem, and the CodeGraph is generated using static analysis.
This CodeGraph is then consumed in CodeScribe, which
uses two additional external information sources: prompts and
configuration files. These are discussed in detail in Section
IV-B. The output of CodeScribe, called “Synthesized Tech-
nical Descriptions” (SynTD), is consumed by CodeContrast.
CodeScribe uses recursive synthesis (shown as “S” in Figure
1) indicated by the self-loop. To enable an end user (or an
external system/agent) to interact with the documentation,
multiple custom agents are built. The end user interacts with
the Master Agent (MA) via an MCP gateway. The MA is an
LLM-based orchestrator that calls multiple specialized agents.
The CodeScribe Agent is an RAG-based system on the SynTD.
There is a CodeContrast agent that can invoke API calls on the
trained contrastive model. The CodeGraph agent can perform
custom traversals on the CodeGraph via an exposed API.
Given a natural-language question from the user (an Engi-
neer in this example), the MA retrieves relevant code blocks
from the CodeContrast agent using Text→Code-based re-
trieval. The MA retrieves the hierarchy of the relevant methods
from the CodeGraph agent and obtains their documentation
using the CodeScribe Agent. Finally, the MA composes a
natural-language response to the end user and adds relevant
diagrams and code blocks to provide a more comprehensive
answer. The end user can interact further with the MA with
follow-up questions. The Engineer can also ask questions, such
as explanations of specific files, methods, or classes, and their
relevance to the overall system. In such a case, MA uses the
Code→Text retrieval from the CM agent. It also identifies the
method or file hierarchy from the CodeGraph agent and the
documentation from the CodeScribe Agent. The MA decides
which type of retrieval to invoke from the CodeContrast agent.
This system allows for seamless end-to-end navigation and
interpretation of the repository.
IV. METHODOLOGY
A. CodeGraph Creation
To create the CodeGraph, a static analysis of the code
repository is first performed. Static analysis identifies all
code files and their corresponding methods. Dependencies
are resolved via compile commands or, if unavailable, with
reasonable heuristics. Node types are files and methods, and
in object-oriented languages, other node types, such as classes,
are added. Comments written by the developer for the methods
are also extracted as attributes for the method nodes in Code-
Graph, along with the method signatures. For methods without
a developer-written comment, an LLM is prompted to generate
one. The actual method body is also available as an attribute
on the method. Since the same method can appear in multiple
files, nodes are named “method_name:::file_name”
where “:::” is chosen as the separator since it is unlikely to ap-
pear elsewhere. In object-oriented languages, nodes are named
“method_name:::file_name::::line number” to handle
operator overloading. Method names include the namespace
and class name, where relevant, as fully qualified names.
The Tree-Sitter library [29] is used for parsing, though other
approaches can be used. The CodeGraph generation, of course,
needs (programming) language-specific parsing. The Code-
Graph structure is generic, and the rest of the processing in
the entire system is language-agnostic.
The CodeGraph is saved as a Python Networkx [30] library
object. This CodeGraph is also exposed through a FastAPI
service [31]. Several endpoints are exposed via the FastAPI
service. Most are standard endpoints for graph traversal, e.g.,
Breadth-First-Search (BFS) and Depth-First-Search (DFS),
along with the “invokes” edge in both forward and reverse
directions. The resultant CodeGraph and the endpoints are
used to generate the documents using CodeScribe.
B. CodeScribe
CodeScribe documentation is driven by the repository’s
directory structure because that is the natural way developers
navigate it. The output of CodeScribe is Markdown files
in a directory structure that replicates the code repository’s

directories. CodeScribe has configuration files that allow one
to exclude irrelevant directories and include only file name
extensions that are present. Every directory can have one or
more perspectives to document the code, called “chapters”
(e.g., code description, algorithms, data flow, interfaces). For
each chapter, a custom prompt is generated, with flexibility to
customize per directory. CodeScribe can also consume config-
uration information, such as abbreviation lists for specialized
domains.
The system prompts are designed with three key principles:
(1) LLM output is constrained to generate documents at
hierarchical levels of abstraction, summarizing at appropriate
semantic boundaries; (2) quoted code segments are marked
with metadata (method name, file path, language) to enable
downstream parsing and tracing back to source; (3) con-
sistency across documentation perspectives ensures coherent
multi-chapter views of the same code units. These design
choices are critical for downstream parsing and contrastive
model training.
When processing any directory, CodeScribe invokes Code-
Graph to find all files in the directory and the methods
they contain. Next, among the methods it identifies, start
methods are those with an in-degree of zero in the method-
only subgraph (a subgraph consisting only of methods). These
methods are invoked by the external system (outside the scope
of the current module graph). For each start method, the DFS
traversal tree is retrieved via an endpoint on the CodeGraph
API. The DFS traversal endpoint generates a key for each
element in the DFS walk, and this information is included
in the LLM’s context. The context also includes the method
definitions in the DFS tree. Thus, there is one Markdown
output file per chapter and per start method. The documents
for each start method are then combined for a summarized
document at the directory level. Optionally, via a configuration
file, summarizations for directory hierarchies are also done.
However, in large repositories, it is common to find trees
that exceed the allowable context window, especially since
method definitions are included. It is important to note that
context sizes include output tokens, and there must be a
reasonable allowance left for the LLM to generate sufficiently
detailed documentation. This requires that the DFS walk trees
be properly chunked. Hence, we build a chunking process
that allows customizable chunk sizes. To handle such large
trees, we implement an algorithm that uses recursive post-
order traversal to process the DFS tree. For each node, we
first process all children recursively, collecting any remaining
chunks. We then check if the current node plus all child
remainders fit within the primary context limit. If so, we
merge them. If not, we finalize each child remainder as an
independent chunk and keep only the current node. Finally, if
the resulting chunk exceeds the primary limit plus a buffer,
we split it into overflow chunks and return the remaining tail.
The chunks are presented to the LLM as context, and the
output of the previous chunk is added to future chunks in
the context in a recursive generation process. The output of
intermediate chunks is temporary and not included in the final

documentation. Our algorithm ensures that when the LLM
processes a parent caller, it possesses a high-level functional
summary of all callee implementations, even if the source
code of those children is not included in the current active
window. This rolling summarization effectively compresses
the global DFS walk state, allowing the model to generate
accurate parent-level documentation without having to guess
the behavior of its dependencies.
CodeScribe can also process incrementals based on git
commit IDs. This process can be done by identifying the last
processed git commit and identifying files that have changed.
Further to this, the methods in these impacted files are iden-
tified and checked against the previous version of the graph
to see if they have changed. If they have, then the root/start
methods of the trees they belong to are identified. This method
is shown in Figure 2. Once this is done, CodeScribe asks the
LLM to modify only the start methods and any summarization
documents generated for this. This process allows incremental
processing at any frequency, from periodic intervals such as
weekly to integration with Continuous Integration/Continuous
Development (CI/CD) pipelines. CodeScribe’s output is then
parsed into a more palatable data format for CodeContrast.
C. Parsing CodeScribe Data
As mentioned before, CodeScribe generates Markdown
output that mimics the repository’s directory structure. The
documents contain a mixture of the following:
• Hierarchical section headers denoting algorithms and
module structure.
• Inline code blocks annotated with method names, file
paths, and programming language identifiers.
• PlantUML
diagram
specifications
embedded
within
fenced code blocks.
• Free-form textual descriptions providing domain context,
algorithmic rationale, and inter-component relationships.
To utilize this data for training CodeContrast, the Markdown
files undergo several processes:
1) Markdown-to-JSON Conversion: A custom recursive
parser was implemented to convert Markdown documents
into nested JSON structures. The headers and subheaders

of the Markdown file become the keys of the JSON file.
Non-header content is aggregated under an arbitrary key at
the appropriate nesting level. This approach preserves the
hierarchical organization of the original documentation while
enabling programmatic traversal.
2) Code Block and Text Separation: Each leaf node in the
resulting JSON tree is processed to separate the code blocks
from the text segments. A regex-based extractor identifies
fenced code blocks (delimited by triple backticks) and captures
both the language identifier and the source code. The remain-
ing text, after code block removal, is retained as a description.
The extraction procedure traverses the JSON tree recursively,
assigning a dot-separated depth identifier (e.g., 1.2.3) to each
node. This depth encoding enables the subsequent identifica-
tion of parent-child and sibling relationships among extracted
entries, which is critical for constructing the relational features
of the final dataset.
3) Code Block Classification: Each extracted code block is
classified into one of three categories based on its content:
• Code: Blocks containing annotated source code with
explicit method name and file path metadata (extracted
via inline comments from CodeScribe).
• UML: Blocks identified as PlantUML specifications, de-
tected by the presence of @startuml directives or the
PlantUML language identifier.
• Pseudocode: Code blocks lacking method name and file
path annotations, treated as pseudocode or algorithmic
sketches.
4) Relational Feature Construction: For each code entry,
the pipeline constructs a rich set of relational features by using
the depth-encoded tree structure from CodeScribe:
• Parent context: Textual descriptions from the immediate
parent node, providing high-level context.
• Sibling context: Method names, comments, file paths,
and code of entries sharing the same parent, capturing
co-located functionality.
• Module-level
context: Aggregated commentary from
text-only nodes that lack direct child code blocks, serving
as overarching module documentation.
These relational features are designed to provide the con-
trastive learning model with multi-granularity contextual sig-
nals linking code to its surrounding documentation. The
parsed records are merged with the call graph data cre-
ated earlier, using the same composite key of the form
“method_name:::file_path”
D. Synthetic Data Generation
Large repositories often have sparse, inconsistent, or out-
dated data (e.g., missing comments, legacy documentation,
or domain-specific abbreviations). Moreover, real developer
queries often take the form of questions rather than direct text
descriptions. Therefore, to improve coverage and better match
downstream retrieval and reasoning workloads, synthetic ques-
tions generated from the parsed records are augmented, with
code included only as a grounding aid.
1) Design Principles: Synthetic questions are constructed
with two explicit objectives:
• Intent diversity: cover common developer intents such
as purpose/behavior, parameter usage, edge cases, and
preconditions, error handling, and interactions within a
local module context.
• Retrieval grounding: include repository-specific termi-
nology (parameter names, types, macros, struct/enum
identifiers, and field names) to improve retrievability,
while explicitly discouraging “keyword dumping”.
In our pipeline, the semantic intent of each question is pri-
marily driven by the available documentation signal. At the
same time, the method signature and a bounded code snippet
are used as auxiliary sources for terminology anchors.
2) Generation Inputs: Each synthetic question set is gen-
erated for a single code entry produced by Section IV-C.
For a given entry, the generation payload consists of:
• Documentation signal: one consolidated text slice cor-
responding to a selected comment level or hierarchical
comment fields when available.
• Code signal: the method signature and a bounded code
snippet (provided for terminology only, with explicit
instructions not to copy verbatim). We provide a signature
with the symbol name removed.
The generator, therefore, receives a comment-driven descrip-
tion of behavior, augmented with a limited amount of code-
local context.
3) Terminology Anchor Extraction: To encourage grounded
and retrievable questions, we extract candidate anchors from
the entry:
• Behavior anchors (BEHAVIOR_ANCHORS): action-level
intent tokens (verbs) that constrain question semantics.
• Parameter anchors (PARAM_TERMS): parameter names
and salient type tokens parsed from the function signa-
ture.
• Context anchors (CONTEXT_TERMS): repository- and
domain-specific terminology mined from the documen-
tation slice and the bounded code context.
• Key terms (KEY_TERMS): a capped union of parameter
and context anchors, used as a lexical grounding con-
straint while limiting the total number of enforced tokens
to avoid keyword stuffing.
4) Prompting Strategy: Comment-Driven Intent with An-
chored

5) Post-processing: We apply lightweight filtering to im-
prove precision and reduce noise:
• Format and alignment checks: enforce strict JSON out-
put and validate echoed tags; discard malformed outputs.
• Deduplication: remove exact and near-duplicate ques-
tions within the same ID.
• Informativeness: discard questions that do not contain
the required anchors or fall below a minimum length.
To assess retrieval generalization beyond trivial lexical short-
cuts, we additionally evaluate a post-processed variant where
function-name tokens are removed from questions.

E. CodeContrast Architecture
CodeContrast is a custom dual-encoder contrastive learn-
ing system [32] that aligns natural-language documentation
embeddings with source-code embeddings. The system is
designed for a code retrieval task: given a textual query (e.g.,
documentation or comments), retrieve the most relevant code
snippet from a corpus, and vice versa. It uses PyTorch’s
Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) [33] for distributed multi-
GPU training, supports both SentenceTransformer (SBERT)
[34] and normal BERT Transformer [35] backbones, and
includes a full pipeline from data preparation through training,
embedding store creation, and evaluation. The full architecture
is shown in Figure 4.
1) Data Preparation Pipeline: This module serves as the
initial stage of the data-processing pipeline. It loads a JSON
input file that is created from Section IV-C, and applies
validation and filtering logic to produce structured entries
containing code, documentation, unique identifiers, and query
types. This induces a one-to-many supervision structure: one
code unit corresponds to many valid textual descriptions:
• a single code unit (method signature and bounded code
snippet), and
• multiple text views (raw documentation, hierarchical
context, and synthetic questions), each tagged by a
query_type.
During this step, the system also flags entries that may
cause issues, such as those with insufficient documentation or
code that is too long to process effectively. Once everything is
cleaned and organized, the module splits the data into training,
validation, and test sets and then saves the final outputs.
2) Core Model Architecture: The embedding system sup-
ports several backbone options. In one setup, we use SBERT
encoders, which produce sentence embeddings directly. In
another, we use Transformer models such as BERT, where
we create fixed-size representations either by averaging the
contextual token embeddings or by taking the final token
embedding. To make sure these different backbones produce
vectors of the same size, we optionally add a projection layer
that maps everything to a shared dimension d. All embeddings
are then ℓ2-normalized onto the unit hypersphere, enabling
cosine similarity to be computed by dot product.
A dual-encoder framework integrates these embedding mod-
els in a unified contrastive learning setup. Each encoder
processes either a text query or a code snippet, and both are
trained jointly using a similarity objective that is adjusted by
a temperature parameter. Because training runs across several
devices, we gather embeddings from all GPUs to form a
single global similarity matrix. This lets the model compare
every item in the batch to all others, increasing the number
of negative examples and effectively creating a much larger
batch. In practice, this leads to more stable training and
stronger contrastive representations.
3) Differentiable Global-Batch Training under FSDP: We
use the Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) paradigm for
training - this runs across multiple devices, so we bring
all embeddings and labels together into one global batch
before computing the similarity matrix. This gives the model
a much larger set of negatives and keeps the contrastive
comparisons consistent across GPUs. To make this work, we
use a differentiable all-gather operation that allows gradients
to flow through the gathered tensors, which keeps the entire
contrastive objective fully trainable even in a distributed setup.
For safety, any rank that produces an empty batch still par-
ticipates in the gather using placeholder tensors. This avoids
synchronization issues and prevents the training process from
stalling.
4) Multi-positive Symmetric Contrastive Objective: Multi-
ple text views may describe the same underlying code unit, and
these code-text pairs may appear multiple times within a batch,
depending on sampling. Therefore, positives using identifier
labels are defined. Let ℓi denote the class label derived from
idi. For each text anchor ti, the set of positive code indices
is P(i) = {j | ℓj = ℓi}. The Text→Code loss uses a multi-
positive InfoNCE objective with log-sum-exp aggregation:

5) Evaluation Metrics: We evaluate retrieval performance
in both directions using metrics derived from the cross-modal
similarity matrix S . For each query, we define the top matches
as the candidates with the highest matching similarity scores,
and report Top-k accuracy. Recall@K measures how many of

direction-specific metrics by evaluating both S (Text→Code)
and S⊤(Code→Text).
V. RESULTS
A. Test Methodology
The objective of the testing phase is to assess how ef-
fectively the model retrieves the correct code function when
provided with a natural language query (Text→Code), and how
well it identifies the appropriate textual description when given
a code snippet (Code→Text). The evaluation uses a held-out
test set consisting of methods paired with their corresponding
text–code samples. Each sample includes a function along with
all associated textual descriptions, such as raw docstrings, brief
comments, self-comments, and synthetic questions. None of
the test methods or their synthetic variants are included in the
training data, which ensures fair and unbiased assessment. Two
types of tests are conducted. The first is the non-synthetic test,

which pairs each code sample with its original human-authored
(or LLM-authored when absent) textual descriptions. The
second is the synthetic test, which augments each original
pair with LLM-generated questions derived from the same
function, as described in Section IV-D.
In addition to testing for the accuracy of CodeContrast, we
also do an evaluation for testing the output of the Code Com-
prehensor system by using LLM-as-a-judge for the output of
the MA. As this is a subjective evaluation, we use the RAGAS
framework [36]. In particular, we use the Answer Correctness
(AC) and Faithfulness (FF) metrics of this framework; earlier
studies have shown that these have the best correlation with
ground truth [37]. This evaluation is done on a subset of
the synthetic questions; the generated answer from the MA
is compared with the ground-truth answer used at the time the
synthetic questions were generated.
B. Dataset
We evaluate our results on two repositories. One of them
(called Repo-A) is a proprietary C-language repository in a
large telecommunications organization, having over 5 million
Lines of Code (LOC) in “.c” and “.h” files only. In addition, to
ensure replicability, we run our experiments using OpenCV2.
OpenCV has about 1.2 million LOC across its ”.c”, ”.h”, and
”.cpp” files. We use Anthropic Sonnet 4.5 as the LLM for
CodeScribe and Anthropic Sonnet 4.0 for all other generation
tasks (missing comments, synthetic questions).
C. CodeScribe output on OpenCV
CodeScribe output quality can be verified subjectively.
Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) have verified the results of
the proprietary repository and have expressed satisfaction with
the output. For OpenCV, the authors did a manual comparison
themselves, as they are quite conversant with the library.
We compare the output with CodeWiki [12], which is
publicly available for OpenCV. For example, in the section
on 3D calibration, one of the important features available in
OpenCV, CodeScribe provides a modular representation of
its important components and discussions on each of them
separately. This is shown in Figure 5, which is much more
informative than the corresponding module3 in CodeWiki.
The documentation is largely correct and useful, but some-
what verbose. This documentation may be very helpful for

D. Computational Efficiency and Costs
The practical deployment of Code Comprehensor requires
an understanding of resource requirements. CodeScribe gen-
eration for OpenCV (1.2M LOC) required approximately 48
hours and $3,200 USD in LLM API costs using Sonnet 4.5.
For Repo-A (5M LOC), the generation required approximately
8 days and a few thousand USD. CodeContrast training on 4
NVIDIA A100 GPUs converged in 15 epochs over approx-
imately 24 hours. Inference is significantly more efficient:
CodeContrast retrieval requires only a forward pass through
the text encoder followed by cosine similarity computation
against pre-computed code embeddings, achieving <50 ms
latency per query. The full Master Agent pipeline (text-to-
code retrieval + context assembly + LLM response generation)
averages 3-5 seconds per query, depending on the result set
size and the complexity of the response synthesis. These costs
are one-time for initial documentation generation and model
training; incremental updates (triggered by code changes) cost
significantly less per month.
E. Configurations
To study how different levels of natural language supervi-
sion influence cross-modal retrieval, we define three dataset
configurations, D1 through D3. Each configuration adds an
additional layer of textual descriptions to the same code
elements. This gradual buildup allows us to clearly observe
how various comment types and question-answer styles affect
the model’s ability to generalize.
1) D1 — Method + Docstring (Baseline Model): This
configuration uses only the method’s source code paired with
its corresponding docstring or brief functional description.
Docstrings provide a concise, developer-written explanation of
what the method does and form the foundational text modality
for contrastive learning. They represent the simplest and most
common documentation layer in code repositories.
2) D2 — Method + Docstring + Self-Comments: D2 aug-
ments D1 by adding self-comments, which were extracted
from the CodeScribe data (Refer Section IV-C). These com-
ments offer finer-grained insights into the how and why of the

VI. DISCUSSION
The results across both repositories demonstrate the nuanced
benefits of incorporating CodeScribe-generated information
into the CodeContrast pipeline. In Table I, the Top-1 accuracy
overall for OpenCV is 66.05% for D2 and is 80.64% for D3,
showing an improvement of 14.59%. Similarly, for Repo-A,
we get 8.72% improvement (67.6% for D2 and 76.18% for
D3). In Table II, for non-synthetic tests on human-authored
descriptions, D2 achieves superior performance: on OpenCV’s
doc_brief_merged category, D2 achieves Top-1 accuracy
of 96.43% while D3 achieves 93.94%. This indicates that
adding parent/sibling context and synthetic QA can reduce

performance when evaluating against developer-authored com-
ments.

This improvement compensates for the drop in accuracy

The larger architecture explains these complementary ben-
efits. CodeScribe introduces a structured way of summarizing
code at different levels of abstraction through call graph
traversal, recursive document synthesis, and chapter-based
documentation prompts. The parsing pipeline converts these
hierarchical documents into structured records that preserve
parent and sibling relationships. These relational signals help
the contrastive model learn contextual relationships between
methods. D2 excels when queries closely match human-
authored documentation, while D3 provides benefits for high-
variability or indirectly-specified queries that require broader
semantic reasoning.
In practice, the expected query distribution should inform
configuration selection: D2 is recommended for applications
where queries directly correspond to method documentation
(e.g., documentation search), while D3 is better suited for
diverse developer queries requiring understanding of broader
system context. The practical deployment should measure
performance on the target query distribution.
VII. THREATS TO VALIDITY
Internal Validity: Our evaluation is limited to two repos-
itories, both in the systems programming domain (C and
C++). LLM non-determinism and the use of different model
versions (Sonnet 4.5 vs 4.0) across pipeline stages may in-
troduce variability. We used Sonnet 4.5 for CodeScribe to
ensure high-quality reasoning over large code contexts, and
Sonnet 4.0 for simpler generation tasks (missing comments,
synthetic questions) to balance quality and cost; this choice
may introduce distributional differences in the training data.
Additionally, the train/test split is performed at the method
level, but parent and sibling context fields in training entries
may reference code from held-out test methods. To mitigate
this: (1) sibling context includes only method names and
brief comments, not full code bodies; (2) the code encoder
sees only the target method’s body, not surrounding context;
(3) removing cross-references to test methods from training
context fields changes Top-1 accuracy by less than 1% on
OpenCV, confirming minimal impact.
External Validity: We cannot claim language-agnostic
generalization without evaluation on Java, Python, Go, Rust,
and other languages. While the methodology (CodeGraph,
CodeScribe, CodeContrast) is language-agnostic by design,
empirical validation is limited to C/C++ systems program-
ming. This is a significant limitation acknowledged in the
Conclusion.
Construct Validity: We evaluate the retrieval component in
isolation using Top-K and Recall metrics as proxies for “code
comprehension.” The final agentic evaluation is conducted
using the RAGAS framework, specifically two metrics: FF
and AC.
Conclusion Validity: The D3 configuration simultaneously
adds both parent/sibling context and synthetic QA. Without
an intermediate configuration isolating each component, we
cannot definitively attribute improvements solely to either
source without additional ablation studies. The lack of fine-
tuned models for agentic evaluation of code-based question
answering may affect the RAGAS evaluation results.
VIII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORKS
In this work, we presented Code Comprehensor, a unified re-
trieval–reasoning framework for understanding large and com-
plex software repositories. The system integrates hierarchical
documentation generation via CodeScribe and a dual-encoder
CLIP model to enable precise, scalable code comprehension.
Our approach systematically combines call-graph traversal,
structured multi-level documentation, and a rich text–code
alignment pipeline to produce a repository-scale knowledge
representation that can be consumed by an agentic orches-
tration layer. Evaluations on two large repositories, includ-
ing OpenCV and one proprietary industrial codebase, show
complementary benefits across different query distributions:
D2 improves retrieval for natural human-authored descriptions
(96.43% Top-1 on OpenCV), while D3 provides additional
gains for high-variability synthetic query scenarios (80.64%
Top-1 on synthetic text→code), with the choice of configura-
tion depending on the expected deployment query distribution.
The Code Comprehensor evaluation shows FF scores above
90%, indicating the quality of the MA-generated response.
Our experimental results are for one C (proprietary) repos-
itory and one C++ repository (OpenCV), both in the sys-
tems programming domain. See Section VII for a detailed
discussion of validity threats. An experimental evaluation
across a broader set of languages (Java, Python, Go, etc.) and
application domains would be important for validating gen-
eralization. Given that CodeScribe relies on LLM generation,
niche languages that are less well-represented in LLM training
data may pose challenges.
Future work will expand multimodal capabilities by in-
tegrating structural graphs, sequence diagrams, and visual
artifacts. This could better capture relationships and control
flows that are difficult to express in text, improving retrieval
relevance. Additionally, using the CodeGraph as an extra
modality would allow the retrieval to be guided by the proxim-
ity of nodes in the graph and not just semantic retrieval. Such
a process would help improve the answer correctness of the
master agent because relevant methods would be retrieved by
the CodeGraph agent. Also, synthetic question generation can

be refined through improved prompting, richer intent model-
ing, curriculum-based generation, and adversarial techniques
to enhance generalization.
